title: Research roundup: 6 cool science stories we almost missed
gist: A monthly roundup of six July research findings: reanalysis showing the Inca 'Boy of Cerro El Plomo' died of blunt force trauma rather than freezing, osteological evidence that Middle Kingdom Egyptian princesses habitually used bows and maces, an amphibious cyborg cockroach with a catalytic oxygen 'diving suit' from NTU Singapore, the first direct image of Betelgeuse's companion star, ancient DNA confirming Grand Duke Francesco de Medici died of malaria rather than arsenic poisoning, and evidence that sperm whales blow bubbles to regulate buoyancy while napping vertically.

insights.claim: Reanalysis of the Boy of Cerro El Plomo, published in Science Advances, concluded he died of blunt force trauma rather than freezing, with no cold-related injuries to his extremities and an unhealed left frontal skin lesion and fracture consistent with a star-shaped mace rather than an accidental fall.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Long-standing archaeological cause-of-death attributions get overturned by CT and osteological reanalysis — a reminder that imaging technology, not new digs, is driving current findings.
insights.locator: Sacrificial Incan boy died of blunt force trauma

insights.claim: CT scans of the Inca boy showed a full stomach consistent with a pre-ceremony feast, a dilated esophagus consistent with vomiting possibly triggered by the head injury, and foot wear consistent with prolonged walking on a pilgrimage.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Multiple independent physical markers corroborating colonial written accounts raises confidence that documentary sources about Capachoca ritual were accurate.
insights.locator: CT scans showed a full stomach

insights.claim: The same team found that neck marks on two girls from Cerro Esmeralda, long attributed to strangulation, were more likely caused by textiles, with hyoid bones intact, unfractured and in correct anatomical position.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A negative finding that dismantles an accepted narrative without replacing it — the honest limit of what the remains can support.
insights.locator: The team also analyzed the remains of two young girls

insights.claim: A Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reassessment of Dahshur burials found Princess Ita died between 24 and 28 with strong upper-body muscle attachments suggesting habitual mace or dagger use, and Princess Itaweret, aged 20 to 34, had healed rib and foot fractures plus bone evidence consistent with skilled archery.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Skeletal evidence of habitual weapon use in royal women revises assumptions about gender roles in Middle Kingdom Egypt.
insights.locator: Ancient Egyptian princesses were skilled archers

insights.claim: Co-author Zeinab Hashesh argues the bows, arrows and maces buried with the princesses were tools they actively used rather than symbolic grave goods, based on upper-limb development correlating with repetitive high-intensity actions like pulling a bowstring.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Reinterpreting grave goods from symbolic to functional changes how an entire class of burial assemblages should be read.
insights.quote: This directly explains the presence of bows, arrows, and maces in the women’s tombs; these were not just symbolic gifts but tools they actively used.
insights.locator: We found pronounced development in the upper limbs

insights.claim: The study combined osteological analysis with X-ray imaging and FTIR spectroscopy of embalming materials, working around the fact that the princesses' skulls had been lost and some bones were not preserved.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Multi-method reanalysis of 19th-century excavations is a cheap source of new findings compared to fieldwork — a durable trend in archaeology funding.

insights.claim: Nanyang Technological University researchers built an amphibious cyborg cockroach by fitting it with a 3D-printed oxygen tank in a soft waterproof shell that delivers oxygen through four tiny plastic tubes directly to the insect's tracheal openings.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Biohybrid robotics is reaching field-relevant environmental hardening, a step toward deployable search-and-rescue systems that undercut micro-robot power budgets.

insights.claim: The oxygen supply works by injecting diluted hydrogen peroxide into a sealed tank containing a sponge soaked with manganese dioxide catalyst, which slowly decomposes the peroxide into oxygen.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A passive chemical oxygen generator with no moving parts or electrical draw is a reusable design pattern for weight-constrained micro-systems.

insights.claim: The core economic argument for cyborg insects is that using the creature's own muscles for locomotion consumes less power than comparable small artificial robots.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Power budget is the binding constraint on micro-robotics; biohybrids sidestep it entirely, which is why the approach persists despite obvious drawbacks.
insights.quote: Cyborg insects use the creature’s own muscles to move, so such hybrids consume less power than small artificial robots used for similar purposes.
insights.locator: Cyborg insects use the creature’s own muscles

insights.claim: The amphibious roach was tested only in a few inches of water and never fully submerged, with future versions planned to add sensors, navigation systems, and extend the diving suit to locusts and beetles.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The honest limitation — shallow water only — marks how far this is from disaster-zone deployment despite the headline.
insights.locator: The cyborg roach worked quite well in test runs

insights.claim: The European Southern Observatory's VLT SPHERE instrument produced the first direct image of Betelgeuse B, providing firm evidence for a companion star whose existence had been predicted for nearly a century.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Direct imaging closing out a century-old prediction demonstrates the resolving-power gains now available from ground-based adaptive optics.

insights.claim: Betelgeuse B was detectable partly because it is far more massive than previously thought — roughly two to three times the mass of the Sun.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A prior mass estimate off by a large factor implies the models used to predict the companion were substantially wrong, which matters for supernova timing forecasts.
insights.locator: One reason they were able to spot it

insights.claim: Full confirmation still requires a direct observation one year later on the other side of the star, after which the open question becomes what impact the companion has on Betelgeuse's eventual supernova transition.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable follow-up observation — the kind of scheduled checkpoint worth watching rather than a vague 'more research needed.'
insights.locator: There is one more step for full confirmation

insights.claim: The 2019 Betelgeuse dimming, once feared to signal an imminent supernova, was attributed by a 2021 study primarily to dust linked to the brief emergence of a cold spot.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A case study in how a dramatic first interpretation of an anomaly gave way to a mundane mechanism — worth remembering before extrapolating from any single observation.
insights.locator: In 2019, astronomers noticed a strange dimming

themes.theme: Ancient DNA settles a Medici mystery

insights.claim: Yale researchers working with a University of Pisa paleopathologist identified P. malariae in Grand Duke Francesco de Medici's rib bones and P. falciparum in his brother Cardinal Giovanni's, confirming malaria rather than arsenic poisoning as Francesco's 1587 cause of death.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Ancient pathogen genomics can now resolve four-century-old historical disputes, and the same techniques underpin commercial paleogenomics and forensic sequencing.
insights.locator: Medici duke died of malaria, not arsenic

insights.claim: The analysis is part of an ongoing project tracking the spread and evolution of malaria from Renaissance central Italy to the 20th century, and is consistent with archival symptom records and the Pisan team's earlier immunological work.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Longitudinal historical pathogen sequencing builds evolutionary baselines that inform how fast drug resistance and virulence traits emerge.

insights.claim: Tags attached by suction cup to 42 sleeping sperm whales off northern Norway recorded bubble sounds and 3D movement, showing whales napping near the surface blew bubbles 11 times on average versus three or four times for those slowly ascending from deep dives.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A clean dose-response between depth regime and bubble count is what turns an observation into a mechanism.
insights.locator: Sperm whales blow bubbles as they sleep

insights.claim: Sperm whales are the only whale species that rests vertically, taking 10 to 15 minute naps head-up, and blow bubbles to counteract the natural buoyancy of heads filled with oil, wax and air.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Identifies an active physiological control mechanism where passive buoyancy was assumed — a template for rethinking other 'passive' animal behaviors.
insights.locator: Sperm whales are the only species of whale

insights.claim: The open question is whether whales consciously choose to blow bubbles, which would imply they sleep unihemispherically like dolphins with one half of the brain conscious.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Distinguishing reflex from volition here would reclassify sperm whale sleep architecture entirely.
